title: Fly Me to the Moon
full_review:
Fast on the heels of Disney/Pixar's masterful "WALL-E" and Fox's serviceable "Space Chimps" comes another creatures-in-space film.

Billed as the first animated feature designed and produced entirely in 3-D, "Fly Me to the Moon" (Summit) aims to bring the significance of the epoch-making July 1969 Apollo 11 mission to today's youngsters through the fanciful tale of three young flies with astronautical ambitions.

 

The trio is led by adventurous Nat McFly (voice of Trevor Gagnon), who rejects the received wisdom that "dreamers get swatted." Inspired by his grandfather's (Christopher Lloyd) oft-told exploit of stowing away on one of pioneering aviatrix Amelia Earhart's daring solo flights, Nat convinces a bespectacled brainiac named IQ (Philip Daniel Bolden) and garbage gourmand Scooter (David Gore) to join him in hitching a ride aboard the spacecraft.

Alerted too late by her younger offspring, Nat's mom (Kelly Ripa) -- whose favorite exclamation is "Oh, my lord of the flies!" -- swoons with alarm at the news, then faints again on learning that the boys will be aloft, not for the few hours they'd originally imagined, but for a full week.

 

Adding to the real-life dangers of the voyage is a fictitious plot by Soviet no-goodniks Poopchev (Ed Begley Jr.) and Yegor (Tim Curry) to sabotage re-entry. But a certain Comrade Nadia (Nicollette Sheridan), whom Grandpa had fallen for back in his globetrotting days, is ready to put remembered romance ahead of Mother Russia and warn him.

Director Ben Stassen's good-natured film features startling special effects courtesy of the 3-D format, with everything from insects to the towering NASA rocket flying off the screen. While children at the screening this reviewer attended displayed audible appreciation for these illusions, they gave equally voluble proof of disinterest in the story and its characters.

Still, "Fly Me to the Moon" provides a painless history lesson and salutary family entertainment, though some parents may not care for its occasional lapse into some crass humor. But there's a most touching bond between Nat and his grandfather and admirable teamwork among the friends, and the film is devoid of violence or frightening peril.

Apollo 11 crew member Buzz Aldrin provides a live epilogue.

The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-I -- general patronage. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is G -- general audiences. All ages admitted.
